cards.explanation: The answer is everyone in the world, rich and poor alike. The writer says, “Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world…” and then adds “…both low and high, rich and poor alike.” That guest list has no bouncer, friends. Nobody gets left off, not even the fella who says he's too busy to listen.

The answer is their wealth. The writer says, “They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches.” So their safety net is a bank balance. That's what they lean on, friends, and they brag about it too.

The answer is False. The writer says, “No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.” A ransom to God isn't something money can cover. The price is just too high for any wallet, friends.

The answer is living on forever without decay. Verse 9 says the payment would be so “…that he should live on forever and not see decay.” That's what people would try to buy, and no payment ever suffices. I'd have paid my whole quarter price tag to skip getting worn down, and it still wouldn't have worked. Money just can't buy this one.

The answer is die. The writer says it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish. Being wise doesn't get you a pass, and neither does being foolish. Everybody ends up in the same line, friends. Nobody gets to skip it.

The answer is that they leave it to others. The writer says the foolish and the senseless perish and “…leave their wealth to others.” All that stacking and saving, and somebody else gets the keys. Nobody gets to carry it out the door with them.

The answer is graves. The writer says, “Their graves are their eternal homes…” These folks had lands that carried their names, and the grave is the address they end up with. I think that's a humbling one, friends. It makes a big name on a gate look pretty small.

The answer is True. The writer says, “But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish.” All the money in the world doesn't make anyone last. That's a hard line, friends, and the writer isn't sugarcoating it.

The answer is False. The writer says, “This is the fate of the foolish and their followers who endorse their sayings.” The followers are named right alongside the foolish, friends. They don't get their own exit.

The answer is Death. The writer says, “Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd.” A sheep follows its shepherd wherever he goes. So if Death is your shepherd, you're being led somewhere you do not want to go. It's a DARK picture, friends.
The answer is False. The writer says, “The upright will rule them in the morning…” The ones who rule are the upright, not the foolish. The roles get turned around, friends.

The answer is God Himself. The writer says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.” Money couldn't pay that ransom, but God can. He alone has the ability to do it. It's a big relief after all that gloomy talk, friends.

The answer is True. The writer says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.” The word surely is right there in the verse. It's a promise he holds onto with both hands, friends.

The answer is afraid. The writer says, “Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases.” A fancier house on the block is no reason to lose sleep. Let the neighbor add a third garage. You're good, friends.

The answer is that when he dies he carries nothing away. The writer says, “For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down.” There's no moving truck for this trip, friends. Nothing he piled up can go along.

The answer is the generation of his fathers. The writer says the rich man “…will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day.” He may have been praised while he prospered, but he ends up with his fathers like everyone else. No VIP section there, friends.

The answer is understanding. The last line says, “A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.” The writer opened by promising wisdom and understanding (Psalm 49:3), and here he lands right on it, friends.
